seoTitle: DKA Management Algorithm: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Dextrose
metaDescription: The ED algorithm for DKA and HHS as Step 2 CK tests it: fluid first, potassium before insulin, 0.1 units/kg/h, dextrose under 250, bicarbonate only under pH 7.0.
h1: DKA and HHS management: the ED algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM or IM rotation with a DKA admission and a resident about to ask what is next: the criteria, the order set, how to run the drip hour by hour, the bedside math, what to say on rounds, and what you will be pimped on. Every dose comes with the line of the guideline it is from.

shortAnswer.text: 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500 to 1,000 mL/h for the first 2 to 4 hours. Insulin waits until fluid is running.
Under 3.5: hold the insulin and replace potassium. 3.5 to 5.0: insulin with potassium in every liter. Over 5.0: insulin, no potassium yet.
0.1 units/kg/h IV. No priming bolus unless the infusion will be delayed.
Once glucose is under 250 mg/dL with ketones still up, add 5 to 10% dextrose and drop insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h. Never stop the infusion for a normal glucose.
Only for a venous pH under 7.0, and only to get above 7.0.
Ketones under 0.6, pH 7.3 or more, bicarbonate 18 or more. Start subcutaneous insulin 1 to 2 hours before the drip stops.
Saline first, insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose stops falling on fluid, osmolality down 3 to 8 an hour, and LMWH for everyone.

checklist.heading: Running the drip: the hourly checklist

items.text: Every 1 to 2 hours: capillary glucose (JBDS: hourly glucose and ketones).
At 2 hours, then every 4: potassium after the insulin starts (JBDS: venous potassium at 1 hour, 2 hours, then 2-hourly).
Every 4 hours: electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH until resolution.
Targets: ketones falling at least 0.5 mmol/L an hour; potassium 4 to 5; glucose 150 to 200 mg/dL once dextrose is running.
Ketones not falling? Check the pump, the line and the residual volume first; if all work, raise the insulin 1 unit/h every hour until the target is met.
Call your senior for potassium under 3.5 on the drip, glucose under 70, a new headache or falling GCS, or no resolution by 24 hours.

present.intro: An example built from this pathway's practice patient at hour 5. Problem-based, so your resident hears the decision at each fork.
present.oneLiner: 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and moderate DKA (venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 11, anion gap 25, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.1) after 2 days without insulin, hemodynamically stable.

plan.lead: DKA, moderate, on the fixed-rate drip.
plan.text: Insulin 0.1 units/kg/h (6 units/h at 60 kg). At hour 5 glucose 196 with ketones 2.4: dextrose added and insulin down to 0.05 units/kg/h (3 units/h). Ketones falling 0.54 an hour, on target.
4.6 on arrival and passing urine, so potassium in every liter, aiming for 4 to 5; recheck 2 hours after the insulin started, then every 4.
Missed insulin; infection and ischemia screened (no fever, clear chest and urine, normal ECG).

Resolution is ketones under 0.6, pH 7.3 or more and bicarbonate 18 or more; then her usual subcutaneous insulin, started 1 to 2 hours before the drip stops, with diabetes education, sick day rules and follow-up in 2 to 4 weeks.

pimp.a: Hypotension in DKA is low circulating volume, and insulin before adequate fluid can cause cardiovascular collapse as water leaves the intravascular space.

pimp.q: Why check potassium before the insulin?
pimp.a: Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level is normal or high, and insulin drives it into cells: starting insulin on a low potassium risks arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness.

pimp.q: Why not stop the insulin when the glucose is normal?
pimp.a: Glucose falls in 4 to 8 hours, long before the ketoacidosis clears. Dextrose is the substrate that lets the insulin keep running until the ketones are gone.
Fluid and insulin resolve the acidosis, and bicarbonate adds hypokalemia, cerebral edema and paradoxical CNS acidosis, with no gain in cardiac or neurologic outcomes.
They underestimate early and overestimate late. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is the test to diagnose, follow and call resolution.

pimp.q: The bicarbonate is 15 but the ketones are gone. Still DKA?
pimp.a: Probably not: large volumes of saline cause a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis in recovery. Mistaking it for DKA delays the switch to subcutaneous insulin.

pimp.q: Why does the sodium rise as HHS is treated?
pimp.a: As glucose falls, water moves into cells: about 1.6 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL fall in glucose. That alone is not a reason for hypotonic fluid.
It is rare in adults but carries about 30% mortality; younger, physically slight adults are at higher risk, and in children it is the leading cause of DKA death.

traps.text: Insulin before fluid. A priming insulin bolus or a bicarbonate push before the first liter is the classic wrong answer.
Urine ketones. They underestimate early and overestimate late; blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is the test to diagnose and to follow.
0.45% saline as the first fluid. Hypotonic saline is never the opening fluid in DKA.
Starting insulin with a potassium of 3.2. Insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias.
Subcutaneous long-acting insulin alone, or 0.05 units/kg/h from the start in DKA.
Bicarbonate for a pH of 7.1. The line is under 7.0, and the goal is above 7.0, not normal.
Stopping the insulin because the glucose is 230. The ketoacidosis is still there.
A CT head before mannitol in a child whose GCS is falling on treatment. Treat first; image after.
Calling DKA unresolved for a low bicarbonate with a high chloride and a normal anion gap. That is saline, not ketoacidosis.
Insulin before fluid in HHS, or switching to 0.45% saline just because the sodium is rising.
No insulin because the glucose is 180. Euglycemic DKA is DKA: insulin plus dextrose from the start.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing DKA?
faq.a: IV fluid. 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500 to 1,000 mL/h for the first 2 to 4 hours, with an ECG and cardiac monitoring. Insulin starts only once fluid is running and the potassium is known.

faq.q: What potassium level is needed before starting insulin in DKA?
faq.a: At least 3.5 mmol/L in the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus. Below that, hold the insulin and give IV potassium first. Older US teaching (ADA 2009) used 3.3.

faq.q: What is the insulin dose for DKA?
faq.a: A fixed-rate IV infusion of short-acting insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h by estimated weight, 7 units an hour at 70 kg. A 0.1 units/kg bolus is given only if the infusion will be delayed.

faq.q: When do you add dextrose in DKA?
faq.a: When the glucose falls under 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) while ketones are still raised: add 5 to 10% dextrose and reduce the insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h, keeping glucose 150 to 200 until resolution.

faq.q: When do you give bicarbonate in DKA?
faq.a: Only when the venous pH is under 7.0: 100 mmol in 400 mL sterile water every 2 hours until the pH is above 7.0. The UK guideline does not recommend it at all.

faq.q: How do you know DKA has resolved?
faq.a: Ketones under 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.3 or more and bicarbonate 18 or more. A low bicarbonate with a high chloride and a normal anion gap after saline is hyperchloremic acidosis, not persistent DKA.

faq.q: How is HHS treatment different from DKA?
faq.a: Fluid alone first, since it lowers glucose and osmolality on its own; insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h only once the glucose stops falling; osmolality down 3 to 8 mOsm/kg an hour; and prophylactic LMWH for the admission.
